transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I guess… I’m here because I just don’t care about anything anymore. Not in the way I used to. I used to have things that made me feel like myself—my art classes, board-game nights with people, hiking when I could actually get myself out, even the idea of getting back to the soccer team. And now it’s like all of it is on the other side of a wall or something.

I mostly just sit in my room, and I know everything is slipping away, like the classes and friends and plans, but I can’t make myself care enough to do anything about it. It’s not even that I’m choosing not to… it’s more like there’s nothing in me that reaches for any of it anymore. That’s why I came in, I think. Because it’s gotten really bad.
Have you ever heard or seen things that other people said weren’t there?

Yeah… I have. It’s mostly a voice. A woman’s voice.

It usually sounds like it’s coming from the corner of my room, not like a thought in my head, but like… if someone were standing right there near the wall, or right next to my bed, talking at a normal volume. It’s that clear. I’ve looked over before because I really thought someone was there, and then there’s nothing. But it doesn’t feel like “nothing” when it’s happening.

She says things like I ruined everything, and that I should stay inside. And I know how that sounds, I do, but in the moment it feels very real and sharp, like I’m being told something I’m supposed to obey. It’s not vague, it’s not like hearing noise through the walls. It’s words. Her voice. And it scares me, but it also kind of… wears me down, because after hearing that enough, staying inside starts to feel like the only safe thing to do.
Have you ever heard that woman’s voice during a time when you were not feeling depressed?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, it’s hard to separate everything cleanly because it all kind of blends together when I look back, but there was a stretch before the depression got as bad as it is now where I wasn’t completely shut down yet.

Like, I could still cook sometimes—not every day, but enough that I was functioning more than I am now. I was still answering friends here and there, even if I was slower or kind of distant. I remember thinking I wasn’t doing great, but I wasn’t in that heavy, bottomed-out place yet.

And during that time, I was already hearing her voice. It had already started. I’d be in my room or in the hallway and hear her, and I would stop what I was doing because it felt so real. And around then I was also really fixated on the hallway lights, like they were signals about me somehow. That went on for weeks, before the worst of the depression really settled in. So… yes, I think I heard it even when I wasn’t feeling depressed in the way I am now.
Was there ever a time when the woman’s voice was happening for at least two weeks while you were not depressed?

Yes… I think there was. Not like I was doing wonderfully or anything, but before the really heavy depression set in, there was this stretch where I was still functioning more than I am now. I could cook sometimes, like actually get up and make food instead of just ignoring everything, and I was still answering friends now and then. Maybe not in a normal way, but I wasn’t completely gone yet.

And during that period, the voice was already happening. The woman’s voice. I remember because I’d be doing something ordinary, like standing in the hallway or trying to make something in the kitchen, and then I’d hear her and just freeze. It went on for weeks, not just a day or two.

That was also when I got really caught up with the hallway lights. I kept thinking they were signals about me somehow, like they meant something directed at me. So… yes, there was at least a couple weeks where the voice was there and those thoughts were happening, before I got as depressed as I am now.
Was there ever a time when the voice and the ideas about the hallway lights were happening while you were not depressed at all?

Not depressed at all… I don’t know if I’d say it that cleanly. I don’t want to make it sound like I was fine, because I wasn’t exactly fine. But there was definitely a stretch before the worst depression set in where I was still able to do things. Like I could cook sometimes, and I was still answering friends here and there. I wasn’t just in bed all the time or completely shut off from everyone the way I got later.

And during that stretch, the voice was already happening. I remember it really clearly because I’d be trying to do normal things, like make food or walk through the hallway, and then I’d hear her and it would just stop me. And the thing with the hallway lights was happening then too. I really believed they were signals about me somehow, like they were trying to tell me something or point something out about me.

That went on for weeks before the depression got really heavy. So… if you mean totally not depressed, I’m not sure I can say that. But it was before the worst part, when I was still functioning more, and the voice and the hallway-light thing were both already there.
Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually high, energized, or euphoric?

I’m not sure. I don’t really think of myself as having times where I’m, like, euphoric or unusually high. That doesn’t sound familiar to me in the way you’re asking it.

I mean, I’ve had moments where maybe I felt a little more able to do things, or less weighed down for a bit, but I don’t know that I’d call it energized or high. It wasn’t like I was suddenly full of confidence or running around with all this extra energy. If anything, I usually feel more like I’m trying to get through things than like I’m on top of the world.

When you say “unusually high,” do you mean like happy in a way other people would notice as not normal? Because… no, I don’t think so. At least not that I can clearly remember.
Did the woman’s voice continue for at least one month?

Yes… definitely longer than a month. It’s hard to even say it like that because a month makes it sound short compared to how long it’s actually been.

The woman’s voice started a few months after my divorce, and it didn’t just happen briefly and go away. It’s been going on since then, on and off but continuing, for… I think about a year and eight months now. Around the same time, I also started feeling like I was being watched, and that’s been part of the same whole period too.

So yes, more than one month. Much more.
Did your symptoms start after your divorce?

Yes… it started shortly after the divorce. Not the same day or anything, but after that, that’s when things really began, and it’s just sort of kept going.

It’s been almost two years now, I think about a year and eleven months since then. I know I keep measuring it against the divorce because that’s the point where I can actually place it in time. Before that, I don’t remember it being like this. Afterward, it started, and then it didn’t really stop.
Have there been times when you were not depressed at all, but you were still hearing the woman’s voice?

Yes. I think that’s actually important, because it wasn’t only when I was at my lowest.

There was a stretch before the really bad depression settled in where I wasn’t, like… okay exactly, but I could still function more. I could cook sometimes, not every day, but enough that it felt possible. I could answer friends’ messages sometimes instead of just ignoring everything. I still had some normal parts of the day, or at least parts where I wasn’t completely swallowed up by feeling depressed.

But the woman’s voice was already there during that time. And I was already noticing the hallway lights and feeling like they were signals about me. That went on for weeks before the depression got much worse.

So yes, there were times when I wasn’t really depressed in the way I later became, but I was still hearing her.
Have the voice and your beliefs about the hallway lights been going on for at least six months?

Yes… yes, definitely at least six months. It’s been much longer than that.

The voice and the thing with the hallway lights both started a few months after the divorce. I remember it that way because the divorce is kind of the marker in my mind, like before and after. It wasn’t immediate, but a few months later I started hearing her, and around that same period I started feeling like the hallway lights meant something, like they were connected to me being watched.

And it didn’t just last a little while. It’s been going on, on and off, for about a year and eight months now. So… yes, more than six months. A lot more.
For at least two weeks, did you hear the woman’s voice during a time when you were not depressed at all?

Yes… I think so. I mean, yes. There was a stretch before the really awful depression came down fully where I wouldn’t say I was depressed like that. I was still able to do some things. I could cook sometimes, not consistently, but I remember making food and feeling like, okay, I can still do this. And I answered friends here and there instead of just letting every message sit there forever.

But during that same stretch, I was already hearing the woman’s voice. It wasn’t something that only started once I got really low. And the hallway lights thing was already happening too — I was already feeling like they were signals about me, like they meant something directed at me.

That went on for weeks before the depression got much worse. So yes, for at least two weeks, I was hearing her when I wasn’t really depressed yet.
During the times when you believed the hallway lights were sending signals about you, did you truly believe that was real?

Yes. I know how it sounds when I say it out loud, like it sounds impossible or like I’m making connections that shouldn’t be connected, but at the time it does not feel like a guess. It feels real.

When the hallway lights blink, especially right after I’ve been thinking about going to the store or leaving the apartment, it feels like a signal about me. Like they know. Like the people downstairs and some of my ex’s friends are tracking when I’m about to leave, and the lights are part of how they’re communicating it or confirming it.

I don’t mean I just get nervous and then think, “Oh, that’s weird.” I mean I’m sure in that moment. I’ll be standing there thinking, okay, maybe I should go get groceries, and then the light flickers or blinks, and it feels directed at me. Like it happened because of what I was thinking or planning. And then I think, they’re watching, they know I’m about to go out.

So yes… I truly believed it was real. I still have a hard time not believing it when it happens.
Do you have unwanted flashbacks or vivid reliving of the divorce?

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean, I don’t think.

I mean, I remember the divorce a lot, and I can get stuck thinking about it, like replaying conversations or thinking about what I should have said or what I missed. But I don’t really have it where I suddenly feel like I’m back there and it’s happening all over again, like a movie taking over or something. It’s more… memories, and feelings, and sometimes they’re really hard to get out of my head.

When you say flashbacks, do you mean like actually seeing it or feeling like I’m physically there again? Because if that’s what you mean, then no, I haven’t noticed that. It’s more that I think about it too much.
Since these symptoms began, has your ability to work, study, or keep up with friendships dropped a lot compared with before?

Yes. A lot. It’s honestly embarrassing to say out loud, because before all this I wasn’t perfect or anything, but I could at least keep things going. I used to take freelance art-education jobs sometimes, like little teaching projects or workshops, and I’ve basically stopped doing that. I just… I can’t trust myself to show up and be normal and organized and safe-feeling enough to be around people like that.

And socially, it’s dropped off badly. I’ve missed community events I used to go to, and I stopped going to soccer. That was one of the few things that kept me around other people in a regular way, and now even getting myself there feels impossible, or I end up backing out.

My friend has been checking on me because I’m not really keeping up with basic things reliably. Eating, showering, just making sure I’m okay in my apartment… it’s not consistent. I hate that I need that, but I do. Compared with before, yes, my life is much smaller and I’m not functioning the way I used to.
Before your divorce, had you long been someone who felt chronically uncomfortable with other people and tended to have odd beliefs or unusual experiences?

I’m not sure how to answer that, exactly. I mean… I’ve never been the most outgoing person, and I’ve had periods where I felt awkward or kind of out of place with people, but I don’t know if I would say I was chronically uncomfortable in the way you mean.

Before the divorce, I think I could still be around people more normally. I could go to things, talk to people, work with people, and not feel like everything had some hidden meaning. I might have been sensitive or anxious sometimes, or maybe a little guarded, but it didn’t feel like my whole way of relating to people was like this for years and years.

And odd beliefs or unusual experiences… I don’t know. I don’t remember having anything like that as some long-standing personality thing before. Not that I can clearly point to. I might have had weird thoughts like anyone does, but not something I was living inside of all the time.

So I guess my answer is… no, not really, or at least I don’t think so. It feels more like things changed, rather than me always having been that way.
Since all of this began, have you been depressed for most of that time?

Yes. I think… yes, most of the time. It hasn’t just been fear or confusion, even though those are there too. Underneath it, or maybe around all of it, I’ve been really depressed. Like heavy depressed. Not just having a bad week or feeling sad about what happened, but this feeling that I can’t get back into my life, and I don’t even really want things the way I used to.

I barely feel interested in anything anymore. Things I used to care about feel far away, like they belong to someone else. I’ll think, “Maybe I should do this,” or “Maybe I used to like that,” and then it’s like there’s no spark in it. No pull. I mostly just feel tired of being awake and tired of having to keep explaining myself.

And there’s this awful thought—not exactly a thought I choose, more like a feeling—that my life is already over. Like the main part of it ended and now I’m just… still here, going through the leftover motions. I know that probably sounds dramatic, but it feels very real to me when I’m in it. So yes, since this all began, I’d say I’ve been depressed for most of it.

It’s been going on since then, on and off but continuing, for… I think about a year and eight months now. Around the same time, I also started feeling like I was being watched, and that’s been part of the same whole period too.

So yes, more than one month. Much more.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms have persisted >1 month (indeed ~1 year 8 months), supporting a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder and making brief/adjustment explanations less likely, but prior candidate list remains unchanged pending clearer characterization of mood episode prominence and duration outside depression.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms began in the context of an identifiable stressor, which would help distinguish an adjustment disorder from a primary psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Did your symptoms start after your divorce?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since shortly after the divorce, about 1 year and 11 months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the symptoms began in relation to the divorce, which is most directly covered by the overall illness duration and onset timing.

patient.answer:
Yes… it started shortly after the divorce. Not the same day or anything, but after that, that’s when things really began, and it’s just sort of kept going.

It’s been almost two years now, I think about a year and eleven months since then. I know I keep measuring it against the divorce because that’s the point where I can actually place it in time. Before that, I don’t remember it being like this. Afterward, it started, and then it didn’t really stop.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been prominent psychotic symptoms outside of any depressive episode, to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from major depressive disorder with psychotic features and schizophrenia-spectrum conditions.
doctor.question: Have there been times when you were not depressed at all, but you were still hearing the woman’s voice?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch before the worst depression set in when I could still cook sometimes and answer friends, but I was already hearing the voice and believing the hallway lights were signals about me for weeks.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether hallucinations occurred during periods without depression, which directly matches psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Yes. I think that’s actually important, because it wasn’t only when I was at my lowest.

There was a stretch before the really bad depression settled in where I wasn’t, like… okay exactly, but I could still function more. I could cook sometimes, not every day, but enough that it felt possible. I could answer friends’ messages sometimes instead of just ignoring everything. I still had some normal parts of the day, or at least parts where I wasn’t completely swallowed up by feeling depressed.

But the woman’s voice was already there during that time. And I was already noticing the hallway lights and feeling like they were signals about me. That went on for weeks before the depression got much worse.

So yes, there were times when I wasn’t really depressed in the way I later became, but I was still hearing her.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms clearly persist for weeks and >1 month outside the worst depressive periods, which rules against mood disorder with psychotic features alone (F32.3, F33.3). No history of mania, making bipolar-spectrum psychosis less likely. Duration and functional decline keep F20.0 and F25.1 highest; post-divorce onset leaves F43.2 as a lower-probability stress-related differential; F21 remains a lower-probability schizophrenia-spectrum differential.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least six months, which best distinguishes schizophrenia from schizophreniform disorder and helps weigh it against adjustment disorder and schizotypal disorder.
doctor.question: Have the voice and your beliefs about the hallway lights been going on for at least six months?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and the beliefs about being watched started a few months after the divorce and have been going on for about 1 year and 8 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the voice and beliefs about hallway lights, i.e. psychotic symptoms, have persisted for at least six months.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, definitely at least six months. It’s been much longer than that.

The voice and the thing with the hallway lights both started a few months after the divorce. I remember it that way because the divorce is kind of the marker in my mind, like before and after. It wasn’t immediate, but a few months later I started hearing her, and around that same period I started feeling like the hallway lights meant something, like they were connected to me being watched.

And it didn’t just last a little while. It’s been going on, on and off, for about a year and eight months now. So… yes, more than six months. A lot more.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been prominent psychotic symptoms outside mood episodes to distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder and stress-related conditions.
doctor.question: For at least two weeks, did you hear the woman’s voice during a time when you were not depressed at all?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch before the worst depression set in when I could still cook sometimes and answer friends, but I was already hearing the voice and believing the hallway lights were signals about me for weeks.
target_item.reason: The doctor is specifically asking whether the hallucination occurred for at least two weeks during a period without depression, which directly matches this requirement.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I mean, yes. There was a stretch before the really awful depression came down fully where I wouldn’t say I was depressed like that. I was still able to do some things. I could cook sometimes, not consistently, but I remember making food and feeling like, okay, I can still do this. And I answered friends here and there instead of just letting every message sit there forever.

But during that same stretch, I was already hearing the woman’s voice. It wasn’t something that only started once I got really low. And the hallway lights thing was already happening too — I was already feeling like they were signals about me, like they meant something directed at me.

That went on for weeks before the depression got much worse. So yes, for at least two weeks, I was hearing her when I wasn’t really depressed yet.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are limited to a reaction to the divorce or instead represent a primary psychotic disorder, by assessing for marked impairment in reality testing or behavior beyond stress-related symptoms.
doctor.question: During the times when you believed the hallway lights were sending signals about you, did you truly believe that was real?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds impossible, but I’m sure the people downstairs and some of my ex’s friends have been tracking when I leave, because the hallway lights blink right after I think about going to the store.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the belief that hallway lights were sending signals felt real, which directly concerns fixed false beliefs/delusions.

patient.answer:
Yes. I know how it sounds when I say it out loud, like it sounds impossible or like I’m making connections that shouldn’t be connected, but at the time it does not feel like a guess. It feels real.

When the hallway lights blink, especially right after I’ve been thinking about going to the store or leaving the apartment, it feels like a signal about me. Like they know. Like the people downstairs and some of my ex’s friends are tracking when I’m about to leave, and the lights are part of how they’re communicating it or confirming it.

I don’t mean I just get nervous and then think, “Oh, that’s weird.” I mean I’m sure in that moment. I’ll be standing there thinking, okay, maybe I should go get groceries, and then the light flickers or blinks, and it feels directed at me. Like it happened because of what I was thinking or planning. And then I think, they’re watching, they know I’m about to go out.

So yes… I truly believed it was real. I still have a hard time not believing it when it happens.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are better accounted for a trauma-related disorder by checking for intrusive re-experiencing of the divorce/trauma.
doctor.question: Do you have unwanted flashbacks or vivid reliving of the divorce?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unwanted flashbacks or vivid reliving of the divorce, which would relate to trauma-related re-experiencing; this symptom is not covered in the provided profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in the way you mean, I don’t think.

I mean, I remember the divorce a lot, and I can get stuck thinking about it, like replaying conversations or thinking about what I should have said or what I missed. But I don’t really have it where I suddenly feel like I’m back there and it’s happening all over again, like a movie taking over or something. It’s more… memories, and feelings, and sometimes they’re really hard to get out of my head.

When you say flashbacks, do you mean like actually seeing it or feeling like I’m physically there again? Because if that’s what you mean, then no, I haven’t noticed that. It’s more that I think about it too much.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a sustained marked decline in functioning since symptom onset, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from schizotypal disorder and adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Since these symptoms began, has your ability to work, study, or keep up with friendships dropped a lot compared with before?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve stopped taking freelance art-education work, missed community events and soccer, and I need my friend checking on me because I’m not reliably eating, showering, or keeping myself safe.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether symptoms have significantly reduced the patient's ability to work, study, or maintain friendships, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes. A lot. It’s honestly embarrassing to say out loud, because before all this I wasn’t perfect or anything, but I could at least keep things going. I used to take freelance art-education jobs sometimes, like little teaching projects or workshops, and I’ve basically stopped doing that. I just… I can’t trust myself to show up and be normal and organized and safe-feeling enough to be around people like that.

And socially, it’s dropped off badly. I’ve missed community events I used to go to, and I stopped going to soccer. That was one of the few things that kept me around other people in a regular way, and now even getting myself there feels impossible, or I end up backing out.

My friend has been checking on me because I’m not really keeping up with basic things reliably. Eating, showering, just making sure I’m okay in my apartment… it’s not consistent. I hate that I need that, but I do. Compared with before, yes, my life is much smaller and I’m not functioning the way I used to.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are persistent odd beliefs/perceptual distortions and interpersonal deficits dating back to before the divorce, which would support schizotypal personality disorder rather than schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Before your divorce, had you long been someone who felt chronically uncomfortable with other people and tended to have odd beliefs or unusual experiences?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about longstanding premorbid personality traits suggestive of chronic social discomfort and odd beliefs or unusual experiences before the divorce, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that, exactly. I mean… I’ve never been the most outgoing person, and I’ve had periods where I felt awkward or kind of out of place with people, but I don’t know if I would say I was chronically uncomfortable in the way you mean.

Before the divorce, I think I could still be around people more normally. I could go to things, talk to people, work with people, and not feel like everything had some hidden meaning. I might have been sensitive or anxious sometimes, or maybe a little guarded, but it didn’t feel like my whole way of relating to people was like this for years and years.

And odd beliefs or unusual experiences… I don’t know. I don’t remember having anything like that as some long-standing personality thing before. Not that I can clearly point to. I might have had weird thoughts like anyone does, but not something I was living inside of all the time.

So I guess my answer is… no, not really, or at least I don’t think so. It feels more like things changed, rather than me always having been that way.

inference.note: Ruled out F21 because there is no longstanding pre-morbid pattern of social/interpersonal deficits with odd beliefs or unusual perceptual experiences; ruled out F43.2 because symptoms are persistent psychotic symptoms with marked decline rather than a non-psychotic adjustment reaction after divorce. Remaining differential is schizophrenia vs schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, given prominent depression but also at least 2 weeks of psychosis outside depressive episodes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether prominent depressive episodes have been present for the majority of the total illness duration, which best distinguishes schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Since all of this began, have you been depressed for most of that time?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Most of the time since this illness took over, I haven’t just been scared or confused—I’ve been deeply depressed, barely interested in anything, and feeling like my life is already over.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether depression has been present for most of the illness duration, which directly matches depressive symptoms being present for the majority of the active and residual course.

patient.answer:
Yes. I think… yes, most of the time. It hasn’t just been fear or confusion, even though those are there too. Underneath it, or maybe around all of it, I’ve been really depressed. Like heavy depressed. Not just having a bad week or feeling sad about what happened, but this feeling that I can’t get back into my life, and I don’t even really want things the way I used to.

I barely feel interested in anything anymore. Things I used to care about feel far away, like they belong to someone else. I’ll think, “Maybe I should do this,” or “Maybe I used to like that,” and then it’s like there’s no spark in it. No pull. I mostly just feel tired of being awake and tired of having to keep explaining myself.

And there’s this awful thought—not exactly a thought I choose, more like a feeling—that my life is already over. Like the main part of it ended and now I’m just… still here, going through the leftover motions. I know that probably sounds dramatic, but it feels very real to me when I’m in it. So yes, since this all began, I’d say I’ve been depressed for most of it.

inference.note: Mood symptoms have been present for most of the illness, with at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms occurring outside a major depressive episode; this supports schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, and makes schizophrenia less likely.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking help today
opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent psychotic symptoms (clear third-person-like auditory hallucination and delusional beliefs about hallway lights signaling surveillance) lasting well over 6 months with marked functional decline. Depressive symptoms have been present for most of the illness, but psychotic symptoms also occurred for at least 2 weeks during periods when the patient was not depressed, which supports schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, over major depressive disorder with psychotic symptoms. No history of manic or hypomanic episodes was elicited.
